#4073. Latest Update: Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) on SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2051 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) on SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2051 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fine-tuning is the process of continuing to train a pretrained large language model (LLM) on a organization’s own data so it adapts to a specific domain, task, or style rather than relying on general-purpose knowledge alone.
  • According to recent reports, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods like Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) have emerged as a practical solution for fine-tuning LLMs to downstream tasks, reducing GPU capacity requirements by updating only a small subset of LLM parameters.
  • Amazon SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization now supports Full Fine-Tuning (FFT), so you can achieve superior model quality without managing infrastructure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fine-tuning is the process of continuing to train a pretrained large language model (LLM) on a organization’s own data so it adapts to a specific domain, task, or style rather than relying on general-purpose knowledge alone. For businesses, the value is twofold. A fine-tuned model delivers measurably better accuracy on domain-specific work while reducing costs: a smaller specialized model can match or exceed a frontier model on your task at a fraction of the per-token inference price. Those savings compound across millions of requests. Fine-tuning has therefore become an essential process for businesses looking to get more value from LLMs at lower costs.

According to recent reports, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods like Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) have emerged as a practical solution for fine-tuning LLMs to downstream tasks, reducing GPU capacity requirements by updating only a small subset of LLM parameters. LoRA aims to strike a balance between efficiency and expressiveness, however, the low-rank nature of the weight update inherently limits the representation power of LoRA fine-tuned models, potentially compromising performance on complex tasks. This trade-off hampers the ability of LoRA methods to capture complex patterns needed for diverse tasks. To address these challenges, Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) updates model parameters simultaneously, overcoming the low-rank limitations so LLMs can fully absorb complex domain-specific knowledge.

Amazon SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization now supports Full Fine-Tuning (FFT), so you can achieve superior model quality without managing infrastructure. There is no GPU provisioning, cluster setup, or distributed-training configuration required. In this post, we explore when and where FFT consistently outperforms LoRA across key benchmarks, examine the spectral properties of model weight matrices that explain this quality gap, provide practical hyperparameter tuning guidelines backed by controlled experiments using SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization, and show you how to get started with FFT on SageMaker AI.

Model customization types like LoRA reduce trainable parameters by freezing the pre-trained model’s weights and injecting small, separate pairs of replacement matrices (called low-rank matrices) into the model layers. This works well for simple adaptations, but the low-rank structure inherently limits the representation power of the fine-tuned model. As tasks grow more complex and datasets scale beyond tens of thousands of examples, LoRA hits an accuracy plateau where increasing rank (and thus trainable parameters) fails to bridge the accuracy gap with standard fine-tuning. This plateau reveals that the performance gap isn’t simply because of fewer parameters. It’s caused by rank deficiency itself. The low-rank patch can’t capture the full complexity of the weight changes needed for deep task adaptation.

However, for complex tasks and domains where large, good-quality datasets exist, full-rank fine-tuning excels by updating model parameters simultaneously. FFT modifies the model’s weight matrix uniformly, using the full representational capacity of the model’s weight matrices rather than restricting updates to a small subspace, and without introducing the abrupt, localized distortions characteristic of low-rank methods. The result is stronger model convergence, better activation alignment across model layers, and a model that faithfully captures both the target task distribution and the richness of its pre-trained knowledge. FFT’s quality advantage grows with dataset scale: at 100K+ training examples, FFT achieved 90.0 percent on LLM-as-Judge semantic correctness across code generation tasks, as shown in the following chart.

Figure 1: LLM-as-Judge semantic correctness by training method as training data scales to 100K+ examples.

Furthermore, the following radar chart provides a holistic view: the base model (inner polygon) indicates consistently low scores across all axes. LoRA (middle polygon) shows strong, balanced improvement. FFT (outer polygon) extends further on every dimension, with particularly pronounced leads on BLEU and ROUGE-2 scores. This multi-dimensional quality lead confirms that it isn’t a metric-specific artifact but a fundamental advantage of full-rank optimization.

Figure 2: Radar chart comparing the base model, LoRA, and FFT across quality dimensions.

The details of how we arrived at these results, the coding datasets used for model customization, and the experimentation process are explained in detail in the following sections.

It has been revealed that in this post we used the Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) technique on a Qwen3-4B base model offered within Amazon SageMaker AI Studio and performed all the fine-tuning experiments using SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization across LoRA and FFT training methods. Within each experiment, both methods received the same prompts, targets, and evaluation code.

For all the experimentation, we fine-tuned the Qwen3-4B base model on the Magicoder-Evol-Instruct-110K dataset, a curated corpus of 110,000 coding instruction-response pairs spanning algorithm design, debugging, data structures, and systems programming. We applied a 90/5/5 split to the dataset: 99,000 records for training, 5,500 for validation to monitor convergence and training loss during the customization job, and 5,500 reserved as a held-out test set for unbiased evaluation of the final model, as registered in SageMaker AI dataset assets and shown in the following figure.

Figure 3: The 110K instruction-pair dataset registered in SageMaker AI dataset assets.

All the model customization experiments in this post were performed on Amazon SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization. Serverless Model Customization on SageMaker AI lets data scientists and machine learning (ML) engineers focus on model fine-tuning without managing infrastructure or GPU capacity planning. You specify the base model, dataset, and hyperparameters, and the service handles compute allocation and checkpoint management automatically in a serverless fashion. The following code snippet highlights one such experiment for launching a Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) job on Serverless Model Customization using the SageMaker Python SDK.

The code triggers a serverless model customization job, shown in the following screenshot, with training performance metrics tracked in the job and viewable in the linked MLflow app.

Figure 4: Serverless model customization job with training metrics tracked in MLflow.

Switching from Full Fine-Tuning to LoRA requires only one change: set TrainingType.FULL to TrainingType.LORA. The rest of the code remains identical:.

We tested the resulting customized models across three diverse evaluation methods built into SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization: LLM-as-Judge, PRIMECODE, and MMLU, shown in the following image. Each targets a different dimension of model quality: semantic correctness, code generation fidelity, and general knowledge retention. Together they provide a comprehensive picture of the model customization quality.

Figure 5: The three built-in evaluation methods in SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization.

It has been revealed that the LLM-as-Judge metric uses a frontier model (in this post, Amazon Nova Pro) as an automated evaluator that reads the model’s generated code alongside the original prompt and judges whether the solution is logically correct. On serverless model customization you can evaluate both the customized model alongside the base model, as shown in the following figure.

Figure 6: LLM-as-Judge evaluation comparing the customized model and the base model.

PRIMECODE is a custom scorer evaluation that measures how closely the model’s generated code matches reference solutions using deterministic text-similarity metrics: BLEU (n-gram precision), ROUGE-1/2/L (recall-oriented overlap), and F1 (precision-recall balance). These metrics are fully reproducible, making them ideal for controlled ablation studies. We used PRIMECODE as our primary metric for surface-level code quality because it quantifies how well the model has learned the coding patterns, formatting conventions, and implementation style present in the training data. A high BLEU score means the model generates code that looks structurally similar to expert-written solutions, as shown in the following results.

Figure 7: PRIMECODE text-similarity scores for the customized model.

Recent findings suggest that MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding) is a built-in benchmark that tests the model across 57 academic subjects from abstract algebra and anatomy to Nutrition and Philosophy. It measures whether the model retains its broad general knowledge after domain-specific fine-tuning, as shown in the following figure. We used MMLU as our forgetting detection guardrail. Fine-tuning on code can overwrite general capabilities stored in the model’s weights. By tracking MMLU accuracy before and after fine-tuning, we can quantify exactly how much general knowledge the model sacrifices for code generation improvement, and whether our hyperparameter choices accelerate or mitigate this trade-off.

Figure 8: MMLU accuracy before and after fine-tuning.

The ease of setup and use of SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization let us perform rapid experimentation without re-provisioning infrastructure. We changed training types between LoRA and FFT, swept hyperparameters, and tested across multiple base models. Over a short time window, we ran tens of model customization experiments across multiple supported base models (Qwen3-4B, DeepSeek-R1-1.5B, Nemotron-30B, Gemma-4-26B), systematically ablating learning rate, batch size, warmup ratio, epoch count, and dataset scale. Each experiment, from job submission to evaluation results, completed in a few hours and the resulting fine-tuned models were automatically registered in SageMaker Model Registry as versioned Model Packages, ready for review or deployment.

SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization supports many hyperparameters. In this section, we explain a few key ones, informed by the series of experiments that we ran across multiple hyperparameter configurations within the previously mentioned code generation task. While effective values will vary by task, the patterns observed across these experiments provide useful starting points when configuring FFT model customization jobs. For more information about the hyperparameters that you can configure before launching an FFT model customization job, see the hyperparameters documentation page.

In full fine-tuning, the learning rate controls how aggressively every weight is updated. Unlike LoRA, where only small adapter matrices change, an FFT learning rate that is too high permanently overwrites pretrained knowledge. In our experiments, the following LR × dataset-size risk map shows that an LR of 2e-5 on a large dataset (over 100 thousand) was the safe zone.

Figure 9: Learning rate and dataset-size risk map for full fine-tuning.

Sources indicate that epoch count in FFT is fundamentally a forgetting question, not a loss-curve question. Training loss will keep falling and your held-out validation will look healthy because it shares a distribution with training data, but capabilities on everything you didn’t train on quietly degrade. The LLM-as-Judge correctness score rose to 90.0 percent at 3 epochs, and extending beyond 3 epochs degraded every variant we experimented with.

Batch size determines how many examples contribute to each gradient step. At a fixed learning rate, smaller batches produce more noisy updates that behave much like a higher learning rate, increasing forgetting risk. Larger batches reduce noise but also reduce the number of optimization steps, potentially underfitting.

Figure 10: Effect of global batch size on model quality.

FFT modifies every parameter in the model, including the parameters that encode general knowledge acquired during pre-training. When fine-tuning pushes these parameters too aggressively toward a narrow domain, the model can “forget” its broader capabilities, a phenomenon known as catastrophic forgetting. We tested for this systematically using MMLU, measuring general knowledge retention across all our fine-tuning configurations. A baseline configuration with warmup=5 percent, batch size 8, and LR=2e-5 best preserved general knowledge (MMLU), as shown in the following figure.

Figure 11: MMLU general-knowledge retention across hyperparameter configurations.

In a recent development, hence, it is vital to note that FFT isn’t universally superior to LoRA, and its effectiveness is extremely sensitive to hyperparameter choices. For example, in our experiments, both FFT and LoRA underperformed the base model on MATH exact match, underscoring the challenge of preserving reasoning capabilities during domain-specific fine-tuning. Aggressive learning rates (LR ≥ 5e-5) in FFT proved particularly destructive, causing MATH scores to plummet to 2–3 percent and MMLU accuracy to drop to 3.6 percent, clear evidence of catastrophic forgetting. Additionally, LoRA slightly outperformed FFT on the LLM-as-Judge metric (81.5 percent compared to 79.5 percent), demonstrating that parameter-efficient methods can still hold an edge on subjective quality assessments. These findings reinforce that the choice between FFT and LoRA should be guided by careful experimentation, dataset characteristics, and a clear understanding of the trade-offs involved.

With Full Fine-Tuning on Amazon SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization, your model can fully absorb domain-specific knowledge when task complexity and data scale demand it. If your use case requires deep adaptation, such as specialized reasoning, code generation, or domain-specific language understanding, and you have sufficient high-quality training data, FFT delivers measurably stronger results.

It has been revealed that you can get started with FFT on SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization with serverless training, built-in evaluation, and without infrastructure or compute capacity planning, so you can focus on your data and hyperparameter choices. You can use the SageMaker Python SDK to configure and launch your training and evaluation jobs programmatically. You can see the documentation for supported base models available for Full Fine-Tuning on Serverless Model Customization.

Human-AI Interactions and Societal Pitfalls

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (141 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2309.10448v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When working with generative artificial intelligence (AI), users may see productivity gains, but the AI-generated content may not match their preferences exactly. To study this effect, we introduce a Bayesian framework in which heterogeneous users choose how much information to share with the AI, facing a trade-off between output fidelity and communication cost. We show that the interplay between these individual-level decisions and AI training may lead to societal challenges. Outputs may become more homogenized, especially when the AI is trained on AI-generated content, potentially triggering a homogenization death spiral. And any AI bias may propagate to become societal bias. A solution to the homogenization and bias problems is to reduce human-AI interaction frictions and enable users to flexibly share information, leading to personalized outputs without sacrificing productivity.

#4066. Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1582 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1582 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral.
  • Sources indicate that there are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team.
  • Recent findings suggest that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:.

Sources indicate that there are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Recent findings suggest that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

It has been revealed that mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

In a recent development, for community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

According to recent reports, mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

Sources indicate that for each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Industry observers note that mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:.

Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

In a recent development, mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

Recent findings suggest that mistral Large 4 is also available on Inference Endpoints, with a ready-to-deploy recipe on 8 x NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The recipe runs vLLM with the FP8 weights split across all eight GPUs using tensor and expert parallelism, and uses the model's built-in DSpark draft head for faster generation through speculative decoding. Industry News: What Does an Agent Need? Bundle-Aware Agent Resource Composition

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (242 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.22030v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: An agent resource's value depends on its backbone and companion resources and is known only after execution. Token-based generators remain tied to their training catalog, while independent resource scoring misses complementarities and reused bundles target other tasks. We formulate Task-Conditioned Agent Resource Composition (AgentComposition): jointly selecting a backbone model and a tool-skill bundle to maximize end-to-end execution utility. Our Retrieval-Grounded Bundle-Aware Agent Generation retrieves candidate resources and past configurations of similar tasks. A fine-tuned generator reads resource descriptions and recombines candidates through constrained beam search, allowing new resources without retraining. A bundle-aware critic ranks complete configurations using a large language model (LLM) teacher and historically successful configurations as execution proxies, and adapts to execution feedback when available. We evaluate reference recovery, offline execution with judged and native rewards, and online recommendation with real execution, building AgentSelect-Exec with 5,060 executed configurations. Our method recovers the complete reference configuration within ten candidates for 67.73% of AgentSelect queries, nearly twice the strongest baseline, and leads all baselines on SkillsBench. The proxy-trained critic raises the top-ranked agent's execution score from 7.58 to 8.37 out of 10; execution feedback increases it to 8.78, above the strongest baselines. Four target-domain queries suffice to adapt the generator to SkillsBench. Agents recommended online outperform the strongest baselines under both an LLM judge and native verifiers. These results support learning and transferring joint resource composition from task experience.

Latest Update: Markets for Compute and Inference: Structure, Financing, and Risk Transfer

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (311 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.20242v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Capacity to run large language models is rented by the accelerator-hour, and their output is sold by the million tokens. Both goods now have published price indices, an over-the-counter forward has traded on one, compute futures are listed offshore, and CME and ICE have specified futures on rental indices that await the United States regulator. We ask what in these two markets can be hedged, by whom, and at what price. Three findings stand out. First, the price that exchange contracts settle on is not the price that drives operators' revenue. The contracts on CME and ICE reference published short-dated rental rates, while most revenue, and with it credit quality, comes from private multi-year contracts whose prices are largely undisclosed. Second, the token price and the rental rate are linked by an identity through throughput and margin, but they are different exposures, so a hedge on the rental rate does not hedge the cost of inference; at the measured capability of GPT-5 the cheapest list price fell by a factor of 17 in twelve months, and by far less at lower capability. Third, the demand for hedging already sits in credit agreements, as the years by which operators' debt outlives their contracted revenue. Filings cannot measure that gap, because debt is scheduled year by year while contracted revenue rarely is, and the one loan that prices it settles the risk by cash prepayment against a model only the parties see. We design a reverse convertible note through which leveraged operators could buy protection against falling rental rates. Its coupon depends steeply on the annualised volatility of the rental rate, which the two public indices put between about 5% and 89% according to how each is built and the horizon measured; across that range the fair one-year coupon runs from 4.1% to 31.6%.

#4062. Using NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning on Amazon EKS

Using NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning on Amazon EKS

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GPU sharing is not new: Multi-Instance GPU (MIG), time-slicing, and Multi-Process Service (MPS) address different isolation and utilization needs.
  • NVIDIA Run:ai is AI workload orchestration software for Kubernetes.
  • NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning adds Kubernetes scheduling integration, enforced GPU-memory limits, and per-Pod metrics to software-based sharing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GPU sharing is not new: Multi-Instance GPU (MIG), time-slicing, and Multi-Process Service (MPS) address different isolation and utilization needs. NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning builds on MPS with Kubernetes-integrated scheduling, per-Pod memory contracts, enforcement, and metrics.

NVIDIA Run:ai is AI workload orchestration software for Kubernetes. Its GPU Fractioning Operator can help several teams share one or two GPUs on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). Notebooks, model evaluations, and small inference services can leave teams waiting even when GPU memory remains available. In this walkthrough’s baseline, the NVIDIA device plugin exposes the single GPU as one nvidia.com/gpu resource, with GPU sharing disabled. Two Pods each requesting nvidia.com/gpu: 1 cannot run concurrently on that node, even when their combined GPU-memory demand fits.

NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning adds Kubernetes scheduling integration, enforced GPU-memory limits, and per-Pod metrics to software-based sharing. The approach applies to NVIDIA GPUs that meet the GPU Fractioning Operator’s hardware and software requirements, including GPUs without MIG. We use one Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) g5.xlarge instance with an NVIDIA A10G Tensor Core GPU as the validated example. Other configurations require compatibility checks and validation.

Recent findings suggest that NVIDIA announced the open source release of NVIDIA Run:ai on October 13, 2026. This example uses two of its four modular components: KAI Scheduler and GPU Fractioning Operator. KAI Resource Management and Workload Map address organizational governance and additional workload types, outside this walkthrough’s scope.

Recent findings suggest that in this post, we show how to build a custom Amazon Linux 2023 (AL2023) image and configure GPU-memory sharing on Amazon EKS. In the validated G5/A10G example, you establish a whole-GPU baseline, give each Pod an 8 GiB memory contract, and verify 6 GiB allocations. You then inspect per-Pod metrics, test rejection of a 9 GiB allocation, and clean up the disposable environment.

Industry observers note that MIG provides hardware partitions on supported GPUs. Device-plugin time-slicing shares a GPU without replica memory or fault isolation. MPS permits concurrent CUDA processes. Fault containment depends on configuration. NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning adds enforced per-container memory limits and supports time-slicing (default) or sm-sharing compute modes. NVIDIA documents separate workload error domains for its default mode and a shared error domain for sm-sharing. These are not security guarantees. This walkthrough tests memory limits, not fault containment or compute performance. A memory limit does not reserve proportional compute.

In a recent development, amazon EKS documents several GPU sharing options: MIG, time-slicing with the NVIDIA device plugin, and time-slicing with the NVIDIA DRA driver and Karpenter. For guidance on choosing among them, see the GPU sharing guidance in the Amazon EKS Best Practices Guide. Choose GPU fractioning when you need enforced per-Pod GPU-memory limits on GPUs without MIG and can run fixed-size GPU node groups.

Recent findings suggest that dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) provides Kubernetes APIs for requesting and allocating devices. GPU sharing and isolation depend on the device driver’s implementation and enabled features. KAI Scheduler and GPU Operator support DRA. This walkthrough uses NvFractions annotations, not DRA.

GPU fractioning can help interactive notebooks with idle periods, short evaluation jobs, GPU compatibility tests, and small inference services. Choose each GPU-memory request from measured peak usage plus overhead, then test latency under concurrent load. The demonstrated density improvement does not establish a throughput gain or a universal cost reduction.

It has been revealed that the following diagram demonstrates the validated single-GPU environment in the US East (Ohio) Region (us-east-2). You use the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), eksctl, Helm, and Packer to build and operate it. The Amazon EKS control plane runs Kubernetes version 1.36 in an AWS managed Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), separate from the customer VPC. It connects to EC2 workers in private subnets of the customer VPC.

An m7i.large system node hosts the operator controllers and KAI Scheduler. KAI Scheduler places both Pods on a tainted g5.xlarge with one A10G containing 23,028 MiB of GPU memory.

Each Pod has an 8 GiB GPU-memory limit and allocates 6 GiB of GPU memory. The GPU worker uses custom AL2023 with the NVIDIA R615 driver branch, NVIDIA Container Toolkit, and containerd. It runs fractiond with Node Resource Interface (NRI) integration and MPS for sharing. The metricsd daemon exports per-Pod GPU-memory metrics.

Figure 1: Validated example of two GPU-memory contracts on one A10G in Amazon EKS.

The walkthrough uses the AWS Samples repository. Confirm the prerequisites and validated component versions, then complete Steps 1 through 10.

In a recent development, use an AWS account with permissions for Amazon EKS, AWS CloudFormation, Amazon VPC, Amazon EC2, Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS), AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), and AWS Systems Manager for Amazon Machine Image (AMI) discovery. Confirm quota and capacity for g5.xlarge, the system node, and a temporary m5.xlarge image builder. Install AWS CLI v2, eksctl, kubectl, Helm, Packer, Git, jq, and curl.

Use your normal AWS credential provider: a named profile, AWS IAM Identity Center, an assumed role, or access-key environment variables. Prefer temporary credentials. AWS_SESSION_TOKEN is required when using temporary access keys. The examples use us-east-2. Another Region must support the selected Amazon EKS version and instance types.

Before choosing another GPU, check NVIDIA’s GPU Operator hardware list, the selected driver’s hardware support, and the GPU Fractioning Operator prerequisites. Hardware support alone does not establish fractioning compatibility. This walkthrough validates the G5/A10G configuration only. The AMI build targets x86_64. Check CUDA compatibility and memory headroom: The two 8 GiB contracts require room for both contracts and runtime overhead. Smaller devices need smaller contracts and adjusted probes.

The walkthrough creates billable resources, including an Amazon EKS control plane, a NAT gateway, instances, volumes, and an AMI snapshot. Use a disposable environment and complete cleanup when validation finishes.

In a recent development, at the time of validation, the EKS-optimized AL2023 NVIDIA image provided R580 and R595 driver branches. GPU Fractioning Operator v0.1.7 requires R615 or newer. R615 is short-lived and is not the GPU Operator default. This example builds a custom standard Amazon EKS 1.36 AL2023 image with AMI-owned driver and toolkit. It does not use an operator-managed driver container on another OS. The table records lab validation, not vendor support certification.

It has been revealed that we validated this walkthrough on October 22, 2026, using NVIDIA driver 615.71.10. On November 18, 2026, after updating the GPU node taint, we repeated every step except the Step 3 image build, using an image with the same driver. The results matched. The table lists the tested component versions, not a permanent support matrix. Recheck the Amazon EKS AMI documentation and NVIDIA prerequisites before changing any component.

Clone the repository, then create a local configuration file from the provided example and restrict its permissions:.

According to recent reports, after cloning, use walkthrough.env for configuration and run.sh for each stage. Generated files and kubeconfig stay in the ignored .state directory. GPU_INSTANCE_TYPE selects the instance type. Changing it alone does not establish compatibility.

Defaults and optional authentication settings in walkthrough.env.

Never commit credentials. The local configuration file is ignored by Git. Confirm the active identity before provisioning:.

Run stages separately to inspect results, or use ./run.sh walkthrough to run through the memory-limit test. Cleanup is always a separate action.

Run the following command to create the disposable Amazon EKS cluster and its system node:.

The command provisions an Amazon EKS cluster running Kubernetes version 1.36, a dedicated VPC with one NAT gateway, OpenID Connect (OIDC) integration, and a private m7i.large managed node.

Selected fields from config/eksctl-cluster.yaml.tpl.

Run the following command to build the custom AL2023 image with the R615 driver branch:.

In a recent development, the script discovers a public builder subnet and the recommended standard Amazon EKS AMI for Kubernetes 1.36 on AL2023. Packer installs the current patch release from the R615 driver branch and the toolkit, configures the NVIDIA runtime, checks package state, and creates an encrypted image. The Region-specific AMI ID is stored in .state/ami-id.

It has been revealed that NVIDIA_DRIVER_VERSION selects the R615 branch. It is not an exact patch pin. The workflow records the discovered driver version with the AMI ID and uses that version in AMI and node-group tags. Read .state/installed-driver-version for the version observed in your build. For production, pin exact packages and the base image in your own build and validate a supported driver-branch upgrade.

You need this step only because the EKS-optimized AL2023 NVIDIA AMI did not include the R615 driver branch at the time of validation. Prefer an EKS-optimized NVIDIA AMI once the driver that it selects for your GPU and the remaining host prerequisites meet the GPU Fractioning Operator requirements. Check the driver versions in the Amazon EKS AMI releases on GitHub. The sample’s scripts currently require the R615 driver and metadata from the image build, so using a stock AMI also requires script changes.

Relevant Packer settings from ami/eks-al2023-r615.pkr.hcl.

Recent findings suggest that SOURCE_AMI_ID and PACKER_SUBNET_ID are optional overrides for an approved base image or builder subnet. Rebuild and test images when the operating system or GPU stack changes.

Run the following command to add a GPU managed node group that uses the custom image:.

It has been revealed that by default, the managed node group uses the custom image and stays at one On-Demand g5.xlarge, the validated GPU worker. A GPU taint excludes ordinary workloads. The script disables eksctl’s NVIDIA device-plugin installation because GPU Operator manages that component.

Selected fields from config/eksctl-gpu-nodegroup.yaml.tpl.

Run the following command to install GPU Operator and inspect the GPU worker’s host configuration:.

GPU Operator 26.7.1 supplies the device plugin and Kubernetes integrations. Its configuration preserves the image-owned driver and toolkit:.

Recent findings suggest that the same command runs a temporary privileged inspection Pod on the GPU worker, prints the host configuration, and removes the Pod. The validated node reports:.

Recent findings suggest that on this AL2023 node, /var/run is a symbolic link to /run. Both paths identify the same socket. Limit privileged inspection to the disposable environment and confirm the Pod is removed.

Run the following command to test whole-GPU scheduling before fractioning is installed:.

Each baseline Pod requests and limits nvidia.com/gpu to 1. The test assumes one available physical GPU with sharing disabled: One Pod runs and the other remains Pending. This demonstrates the whole-device scheduling constraint before fractioning is installed. On multi-GPU nodes, adapt this baseline and verify that both fractional workloads use the same GPU.

The script checks this state and removes both baseline Pods.

Run the following command to install KAI Scheduler, which includes GPU Fractioning Operator:.

According to recent reports, the pinned KAI Scheduler 0.18.5 chart includes GPU Fractioning Operator 0.1.7. The values turn on NvFractions and per-Pod metrics while retaining GPU-stack version checks. The optional nvidia.com/container..gpu-compute.mode annotation selects compute mode. These workloads leave the default unchanged.

Relevant fields from helm/kai-values.yaml.

In the validation, FractiondReady, MpsdReady, and Ready are True. DriverUpgradeInProgress is False with reason NoDriverUpgrade, consistent with the AMI retaining driver ownership.

Run the following command to deploy two Pods with 8 GiB GPU-memory contracts:.

Each Pod requests and limits memory to 8 GiB and selects kai-scheduler. Neither requests a whole nvidia.com/gpu resource. The repository applies these scheduling fields and runs a CUDA probe that allocates 6 GiB:.

Essential fields from kubernetes/fraction-8gi-pods.yaml.

According to recent reports, the script verifies matching node names and GPU UUIDs. In the validation, both Pods see 8,192 MiB and report allocation_succeeded_mib=6144. Those checks establish placement on one physical GPU, the bounded device view, and successful allocations within each contract.

Measured allocation output from each Pod.

Observe memory while both Pods remain active.

The gpu_fractioning_gpu_memory_used_bytes metric attributes memory by Pod and GPU UUID. The observed 6,394 MiB (about 6.24 GiB) per Pod exceeds the probe’s 6,144 MiB allocation by 250 MiB. Metrics can include CUDA context and runtime overhead. This experiment does not measure that breakdown. Retain workload identity and request, limit, and usage values together when monitoring the shared device.

Run the following command to test an allocation that exceeds the 8 GiB contract:.

Recent findings suggest that this command removes the positive-test Pods and creates one Pod with an 8 GiB contract that attempts a 9 GiB allocation. The probe reports:.

Measured negative-test Pod status.

In a recent development, here, cudaMalloc returns an out-of-memory error, which the probe handles before exiting with code 0. Completed is expected, not OOMKilled. This demonstrates allocation rejection, not container termination or general fault isolation.

Recent findings suggest that capture the VPC ID before deleting the cluster. The independent checks that follow use the default cluster name and Region. Substitute your configured values if you changed them.

Remove the disposable environment.

Standard cleanup removes the test namespace, Helm releases, and disposable cluster while preserving the custom AMI and its Amazon EBS snapshot.

Expect explicit resource-not-found responses for deleted resources. Authentication or permission errors do not establish deletion. Also inspect remaining node groups and cluster-tagged instances. If cleanup fails, inspect CloudFormation events and resolve owned dependencies before retrying. An absent Amazon EKS endpoint does not prove that its VPC is gone.

Use ./run.sh cleanup-all only when the custom AMI and its Amazon EBS snapshot are no longer needed. If image deletion is refused, confirm the AMI ID and sample ownership tag. Do not bypass the safeguard.

Industry observers note that treat this as a behavior validation. Use trusted workloads and apply least-privilege IAM, namespace controls, approved images, and admission rules for fraction requests. Choose whole GPUs or MIG on supported hardware when stronger isolation is required.

In a recent development, the pinned fractioning daemons use privileged containers, host PID access, and NRI/MPS host mounts. Restrict their deployment and configuration to trusted administrators.

Allow headroom for CUDA contexts, caches, batching, and runtime overhead. Measure latency and throughput under concurrent load. Monitor allocation failures, MPS health, NRI connectivity, and GPU errors. Pin the base AMI, driver, toolkit, device plugin, operator, scheduler, and workload images as one tested combination. Rebuild images and test rollback before rollout.

According to recent reports, this walkthrough requires pre-provisioned GPU capacity. It does not configure or validate GPU-fraction-aware autoscaling. The fractional Pods select kai-scheduler, request no nvidia.com/gpu resource, and use a nodeSelector that targets a node group fixed at one node. Karpenter support for secondary schedulers is an open feature request (issue #742 on GitHub). The custom image cannot run on Amazon EKS Auto Mode-managed nodes, because Auto Mode selects and manages their AMI. A cluster can mix Auto Mode-managed nodes with managed node groups, but we did not validate this walkthrough in such a cluster.

Teams that use Karpenter can reference the same custom AMI by ID in an EC2NodeClass. The autoscaling limit still applies. We did not validate this path.

KAI Scheduler is a second scheduler. It handles queueing and placement for Pods that select it. If you already use Kueue, decide which component owns queueing for GPU workloads before you adopt KAI Scheduler.

Recent findings suggest that we recommend running the Amazon EKS node monitoring agent on GPU nodes. In a November 18, 2026 regression run, the agent ran on the custom R615 image with MPS sharing active and reported healthy GPU conditions throughout the sharing and limit tests. That run did not test fault detection. Because GPU Operator already runs a Data Center GPU Manager (DCGM) host engine, configure the agent to use that host engine instead of its bundled one.

In this post, we showed how to configure GPU-memory fractioning on Amazon EKS with a custom AL2023 image, using G5/A10G as the validated example. The approach extends to compatible NVIDIA GPUs after checking prerequisites and validating the selected configuration. You established the whole-GPU baseline, ran two bounded workloads on the same GPU, inspected per-Pod memory usage, and verified rejection of an allocation above the limit. Fractioning can improve access to existing capacity when workload memory fits. Production adoption also requires isolation controls and performance testing.

To repeat the experiment, clone the AWS Samples repository and compare your results with its validated evidence. Explore the GPU Fractioning Operator documentation and the Amazon EKS accelerated AMI guidance before adapting the example to your workloads.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (275 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.22017v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent Skills, file-based packages of procedural knowledge that a coding agent can discover and load on demand, are now shipped by every major agent harness, yet the evidence for how much they help comes almost entirely from settings in which the right Skill is hand-picked for the task and the agent starts from a blank slate. Neither holds in deployment, where an agent chooses from whatever library happens to be installed and frequently carries memory from earlier work. We present SkillBuffBench, a benchmark and paired evaluation protocol that treats Skill access as a three-level factor (no Skill, a curated Skill, and automatic invocation from an installed library), crosses it with memory (off and on), with four agent harnesses and with multiple models (the state-of-the-art proprietary models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, and the state-of-the-art open-weight models from Chinese providers), every model being run under every harness, and evaluates the result on research tasks contributed by domain experts together with the Skills they use, right now in materials science and biology, with the suite extended on a rolling basis. Every run is marked by a deterministic verifier; uncertainty is reported with a paired, task-level bootstrap; and cost, agent rounds and wall-clock time are reported alongside the score rather than folded into it. This version of the paper describes the design of the benchmark, its evaluation protocol and its current tasks and Skills. The evaluation is in progress: results will be added once the runs are complete, and the task suite, results and analysis will continue to be updated on a rolling basis.

The effect of policy cancellation on the risk of an insurance portfolio

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (217 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.18660v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For an insurance portfolio modelled by a large number of i.i.d. losses, the average loss converges to its expected value by the law of large numbers, reflecting the diversification effect of pooling risks. Policy cancellations reduce the portfolio size and thereby weaken this effect. We quantify the resulting increase in risk by applying risk measures to the average loss before and after the cancellation of policies. For a portfolio of size $n$, we show that the impact of cancelling a single contract is of order $n^{-3/2}$, while the cancellation of a fixed proportion of contracts has an effect of order $n^{-1/2}$. We further extend the proportional cancellation regime to heterogeneous portfolios with different cancellation rates and risk characteristics across segments. These asymptotic results provide a quantitative basis for assessing surrender fees and cancellation costs from the insurer's perspective. We complement the theoretical analysis with numerical results for representative life insurance products, illustrating the magnitude of cancellation costs and the effect of portfolio aggregation. The two regimes require different techniques. For the cancellation of a fixed proportion of contracts, we employ central limit theorems in Wasserstein distance. For the cancellation of a single contract, we combine Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality with higher-order distributional approximations based on the Edgeworth and Cornish-Fisher expansions.

Industry observers note that cybersecurity is a fast-growing field, with a constant need for skilled professionals. But unlike other professions — like medicine or aviation — there’s no clear-cut pathway to qualifying for cybersecurity positions. For employers and job seekers alike, this can make the journey to building a team (or entering a successful cybersecurity career) feel uncertain.

Enter the registered apprenticeship program — a proven method for developing skilled talent in cybersecurity that benefits both the employer and the newly introduced professional. Let’s commit to supporting this vital talent development approach as we celebrate National Apprenticeship Week from November 17-23, 2024.

What Is a Cybersecurity Apprenticeship?

It has been revealed that an apprenticeship is a paid, on-the-job training program where individuals learn essential skills while working alongside experienced professionals. Unlike traditional education paths, apprenticeships combine the best of both worlds: earn-while-you-learn, with real-world experience in the field. The apprentice is guided by a mentor and can expect to gain expertise over one to two years, often culminating in a full-time permanent job offer.

In a recent development, much like a medical resident or an aviation trainee, a cybersecurity apprentice benefits from structured, hands-on learning, with mentorship ensuring they develop the technical and workplace skills and gain the confidence needed to succeed. Successful apprenticeship program completers also earn one or more portable, nationally-recognized and industry-valued credentials or certifications. “The apprenticeship program has allowed me entry into a field/position that most can't break into without a 4-year degree,” said Brittany Patterson-Morris, an apprentice with Interapt, an IT services apprenticeship program.

Why Cybersecurity Apprenticeships Matter.

In 2023, nearly 61,000 individuals participated in a registered cybersecurity apprenticeship program in the U.S., a 254% increase in just five years, according to the Department of Labor (DOL)’s Office of Apprenticeship. This growth reflects a fundamental shift in how we prepare the next generation of cybersecurity professionals. As Carla Miller from Albireo Energy puts it, "It’s what we need to expand the workforce.”[1].

For employers, apprenticeships can be an affordable way to build a workforce from the ground up, ensuring that upcoming hires are trained with the specific skills they need. Chris Dunn, founder of Covered 6, shares, “Our cybersecurity apprenticeship programs have helped us attract passionate candidates while lowering the time and cost barriers of traditional training.”[2] Employers can also use apprenticeships to upskill current employees, providing a career pathway to retain proven workers. For job seekers, apprenticeships offer a direct pathway to a career, complete with certifications and mentorship. “The key is blending intensive on-the-job practice with high-quality, up-to-date asynchronous learning," says Ximena Gates, CEO of BuildWithin, an apprenticeship management software manufacturer built by former apprentices. “This is ideal for career changers and those without technical backgrounds as skills can transfer from other disciplines.”.

It has been revealed that A way that employers can fast track a newly introduced program is to partner with an intermediary. As the DOL National Industry Intermediary for Cybersecurity Apprenticeship Expansion, Safal Partners helps employers more swiftly, easily, and effectively navigate Registered Apprenticeships. “Employers of any size can join our already-approved National Registered Apprenticeship program, access no-cost apprenticeship expertise to build or expand their own program, utilize industry-built online coursework for their apprentices, and get ongoing program support to fund, modify, and sustain their program,” said Katie Adams, chief delivery officer at Safal Partners.

Whether you're an employer looking to tap into the growing talent pool or a job seeker eager to launch a cybersecurity career, there are many resources to help. For example, you can:.

By investing in apprenticeships, you’re not only supporting the next wave of cybersecurity professionals, but you’re also helping ensure your organization stays ahead in a field that’s more crucial than ever.

Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1311 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.
  • Sources indicate that today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research.
  • The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Sources indicate that today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

According to recent reports, participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

In a recent development, the U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Sources indicate that project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

In a recent development, the pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many fresh science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Figure 1. Upcoming public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

In a recent development, when organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support upcoming research that others can build upon.

According to recent reports, this is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

According to recent reports, making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an vital first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

According to recent reports, to explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:.

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that the inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

According to recent reports, participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge.

It has been revealed that the CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be confirmed through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or organization building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

Sources indicate that we also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

On Formal Counterfactual Explanations

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (197 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.22010v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Counterfactual explanations are often seen as counterfactual conditionals under closest-world semantics, requiring one to reason over all minimally distant counterexamples. In contrast, formal XAI typically relies on feature-based abductive explanations (AXps) and contrastive explanations (CXps), which admit efficient computation and a minimal hitting-set duality. This paper bridges these perspectives by (i) characterizing closest-world counterfactual explanations explicitly as a disjunctive normal form over all minimally distant counterexample instances, and (ii) introducing conjunctive counterfactual explanations (CFXps), a subclass of counterfactual antecedents restricted to conjunctions of feature literals that guarantee prediction change. The paper establishes structural results connecting CXps, AXps and CFXps: every CXp induces an AXp for its witness instance, and every CXp together with a witness AXp induces a CFXp whose support is precisely determined by that AXp. These theoretical results yield a modular approach for computing CFXps using existing AXp/CXp machinery. Experiments on a representative set of benchmarks using tree ensembles and neural networks show that CFXp extraction is practically efficient. Compared with popular point-based counterfactual explainers, CFXps generally require no more feature changes and can guarantee the counterfactual prediction beyond a single instance.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.16540v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Portfolio outcomes may depend as much on trading restrictions as on how returns are modeled. We compared historical moving-window returns with conditional scenarios from ARMA--GARCH models and a Student-$t$ copula for 30 U.S.-listed exchange-traded funds. Matched mean--variance and conditional value-at-risk portfolios were evaluated under long-only and limited long--short bounds over 946 sessions. Historical portfolios had higher observed reward--risk ratios in most comparisons, but no paired difference remained significant after multiple-testing adjustment. Conditional scenarios did not consistently reduce realized downside risk. We distinguished changes in target weights from trades required to rebalance holdings after market movements. Relaxing the target-adjustment limit changed exposures, turnover, and some returns more than varying scenario count or seed in the examined tests. These findings suggest that assessments of conditional return inputs should consider portfolio constraints and trading requirements.

  • It has been revealed that dialog-RSN-1 is the first PolyAI model available through AWS Marketplace.
  • All in a single pass, Dialog-RSN-1 perceives a caller’s audio directly, reasons about what they need, and responds in real time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dialog-RSN-1, a reasoning model built for real-time complex dialog, is available today on AWS Marketplace and Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. It powers frontier dialog: agents that hear a live call, reason about it, and act in real time.

It has been revealed that dialog-RSN-1 is the first PolyAI model available through AWS Marketplace. It runs inside your own AWS environment on the same AWS cloud that powers PolyAI’s compute and model training and serving.

All in a single pass, Dialog-RSN-1 perceives a caller’s audio directly, reasons about what they need, and responds in real time. On SageMaker, it deploys as an endpoint like other models you run there. It is reachable from your own architecture, billed through your AWS account, and covered by the same virtual private cloud (VPC), AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, and monitoring you already have in place.

You keep ownership of orchestration, telephony integration, and business logic. Dialog-RSN-1 takes off your plate the hardest part to build yourself: understanding a live call and responding to it in real time. The endpoint speaks the OpenAI Realtime protocol, so an existing Realtime client connects through PolyAI’s bridge by changing its base URL. Audio in is 16-bit PCM mono at 16 or 24 kHz (transcode G.711 or Opus first). Connections last up to 30 minutes, and the model is English-only today.

To get started, find Dialog-RSN-1 on AWS Marketplace, then deploy it straight into an Amazon SageMaker endpoint in your own account. Or you can deploy directly from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart.

With Dialog-RSN-1 now onboarded to SageMaker JumpStart, deploying Dialog-RSN-1 takes one click. From the Amazon SageMaker AI console, open the Model Hub, select Dialog-RSN-1 from the JumpStart catalog, and choose Deploy. SageMaker JumpStart then spins up a real-time inference endpoint on a serving stack it has already tuned for you. No containers to wrangle, no instance types to second-guess, and no manual benchmarking. For automated workflows, the same one-click deployment also runs in a few lines of the SageMaker Python SDK.

The Dialog-RSN-1 endpoint runs entirely within your own AWS account. It is deployed in your VPC, accessed through your IAM roles, and monitored with the same Amazon CloudWatch logging and metrics you use for every other workload. Because inference happens inside your account, your callers’ audio and transcripts stay within a boundary you control. For a model handling live customer conversation, this helps support your data residency and auditability requirements.

Sources indicate that models built for live calls may make you choose between speed and understanding. And models built for speed may miss the meaning, and ones built for reasoning may lead to wait time for callers. Dialog-RSN-1 avoids the tradeoff.

With PolyAI, you can build dialog agents that hear and handle calls the way your human agents would. These agents catch hesitation, hear frustration before it escalates, and know when to speak.

In a recent development, real-time customer conversation is the job PolyAI’s Dialog-RSN-1 is built for, and it is already handling live calls in production today. Because the model reasons directly over the caller’s audio, it picks up tone, hesitation, and timing, the signals a plain transcript loses, and decides for itself the right moment to respond.

Dialog-RSN-1 is a model focused on real-time conversations. There is no separate speech-to-text step and no reasoning model on the appropriate moment to talk, so thereby no multiple handoffs.

In practice, that means the callers get responses faster:.

Amazon SageMaker JumpStart is the machine learning hub inside Amazon SageMaker AI, and it exists to collapse the distance between choosing a model and running it in production. For Dialog-RSN-1, that means the frontier of real-time dialog is a few clicks away. You can discover it, prove it on your own data, and ship it to a secure endpoint, all in one place. Here is what you get.

Recent findings suggest that dialog-RSN-1 indicates up in the SageMaker JumpStart catalog with overview and sample notebooks in one place, so your team can understand the model before spending a dollar on infrastructure. To try the model on your own calls, deploy the endpoint and run PolyAI’s sample notebook, which streams recorded caller audio and prints the model’s turn decisions, replies, and transcripts.

From the same model card you choose Deploy, and Amazon SageMaker JumpStart stands up a real-time inference endpoint with a pre-configured serving stack. There is no manual container selection or instance guesswork. The real convenience is the named optimization profiles: instead of hand-tuning infrastructure, you pick the target that matches how you run Dialog-RSN-1. Latency optimized minimizes Time to First Token for interactive, real-time calls. Throughput optimized maximizes tokens per second for high call volumes. Cost optimized minimizes infrastructure cost per request. Balanced is an even tradeoff for general-purpose use.

Because Dialog-RSN-1 is built to respond in real time, you can use the latency-optimized profile to carry that responsiveness straight to your own endpoint. Before you deploy, SageMaker JumpStart surfaces the key performance metrics: P50 latency, Time to First Token, and throughput. This lets you right-size the ml.* instance for your traffic instead of benchmarking dozens of combinations by hand. You can run the whole flow from the console, or script it through the SageMaker Python SDK to wire deployments into continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD).

The endpoint runs inside your own account boundary: in your VPC, under your IAM roles, with the CloudWatch logging and metrics you already have in place. For a model handling live customer conversations, that means your call audio and transcripts stay in an environment you control, which keeps data residency and auditability straightforward.

The result is a frontier voice model that deploys like the other workloads your machine learning team already runs, using the same hub, the same discovery and evaluation tools, and the same security posture. The hard part is the conversation Dialog-RSN-1 handles, not the infrastructure behind it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding latest expertise on a single endpoint.

Industry observers note that granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

In a recent development, while we are excited about these latest features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this upgrade. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

It has been revealed that this pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the latest multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.
