Latest Update: Transformers Model Integration Contracts

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1324 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, on July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5.
  • Recent findings suggest that when we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them.
  • According to recent reports, transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is significant: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

Recent findings suggest that when we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

According to recent reports, transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is significant: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

According to recent reports, the integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

It has been revealed that our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

According to recent reports, transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:.

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

Recent findings suggest that A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

Industry observers note that for example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:.

Recent findings suggest that it also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

Industry observers note that A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

It has been revealed that we replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

In a recent development, one detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

Sources indicate that we then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

Industry observers note that the first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

Recent findings suggest that the Llama 4 Scout shrink report indicates what this looks like on a massive model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Sources indicate that our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:.

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a fresh model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

Industry observers note that we used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

Recent findings suggest that with random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:.

Recent findings suggest that the Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

Recent findings suggest that so we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

It has been revealed that as of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:.

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

#4040. Protect agent tool calls with Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1212 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Protect agent tool calls with Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1212 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in this post, we show how Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway keep sensitive data out of the tools your AI agents call, and out of the model context those tools feed.
  • Skyflow is available in AWS Marketplace, and the interceptor is open source on GitHub.
  • Recent findings suggest that agents have moved from answering questions to taking action, and they take action through tools: Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, SaaS APIs, document stores, and web search.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in this post, we show how Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway keep sensitive data out of the tools your AI agents call, and out of the model context those tools feed. We add Skyflow Detect to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway as a request and response interceptor. The Skyflow interceptor de-identifies data before it reaches a tool, restores it before the agent reads the result, and replaces documents with clean copies before the agent opens them. Your agents and tools don’t change.

Skyflow is available in AWS Marketplace, and the interceptor is open source on GitHub.

Recent findings suggest that agents have moved from answering questions to taking action, and they take action through tools: Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, SaaS APIs, document stores, and web search. Every agent tool call is a data flow. Most enterprise controls cover what goes into and comes out of the model. Far fewer cover what an agent sends to its tools or what those tools send back.

That gap reveals up in three ways:.

Sources indicate that patching each agent doesn’t scale across teams and frameworks, and it can’t reach third-party tools. The controls need to sit where every tool call passes, so authorization, content safety, and data protection apply the same way to every agent and tool.

AgentCore Gateway is that place. It fronts every tool an agent uses, whatever framework or model the agent runs on. It does more than route that traffic. With AgentCore Gateway interceptors, you can run your own code, as an AWS Lambda function, on every call that passes through it. A request interceptor sees each call before it reaches a tool, and a response interceptor sees each result before it reaches the agent. Either one can inspect the payload, rewrite it, or block the call. That makes the gateway a natural place to add data protection alongside Policy and Guardrails. This single control, attached once, covers every agent and every tool behind the gateway, without any change to agent or tool code.

Industry observers note that consider a large European bank with retail and corporate banking operations and strict data-residency obligations. Its operations teams are adopting agents to investigate card disputes.

It has been revealed that an analyst asks the agent to look into a disputed transaction. The agent searches the web for the merchant, then pulls the dispute case note from Amazon S3 to summarize it. Without protection, three things happen:.

With the Skyflow interceptor on the gateway, the same workflow plays out differently:.

The Skyflow interceptor is a single AWS Lambda function attached to both of the AgentCore Gateway interception points:.

It has been revealed that at each point, it calls Skyflow Detect to find sensitive entities such as names, email addresses, phone numbers, government IDs, card numbers, dates of birth, and locations. It replaces them with tokens, or restores the originals. Skyflow Vault stores the original values so authorized systems can reverse the tokens.

The Skyflow gateway configuration decides, for each tool, which of three protection modes applies: Shield the tool, Shield the model, and Shield the document.

Four properties matter in production:.

The reference architecture shows where each component sits. The three walkthroughs after it follow a single tool call through the Shield the tool and Shield the document modes.

The following diagram demonstrates how the interceptor sits between AgentCore Gateway and your tools.

Figure 1: Reference architecture. The numbered steps match the following flow.

In a recent development, the agent runs on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Alongside that flow, the interceptor reads its policy from Parameter Store and its Skyflow API key from Secrets Manager, and it logs each decision to Amazon CloudWatch. It calls Skyflow Detect and Skyflow Vault in an approved Region to de-identify and re-identify data. The targets sit outside the gateway: a third-party web search MCP server, a case-note store in Amazon S3, and a model in Amazon Bedrock that the gateway reaches through an inference target. For model calls, the interceptor keeps a short-lived record in Amazon DynamoDB of which tokens each call minted, so it restores only those. The record holds no original values. For documents, Skyflow Detect fetches the file directly through a presigned URL, so the file bytes never pass through Lambda.

In a recent development, this is the web search from the dispute example, step by step. The customer’s name leaves as a token and comes back as the real value, so the search provider never sees it and the analyst still does.

In a recent development, figure 2: Shield the tool. The customer name is replaced with a vault token before the search provider sees the query, and restored before the agent reads the results.

Industry observers note that this is the analyst asking the agent to draft a reply to the customer. The customer’s name and email address reach the model as tokens, and the draft comes back with the real values in place.

Figure 3: Shield the model. The interceptor de-identifies the prompt and the conversation history before the model reads them, and restores the tokens it minted for that call before the agent reads the answer.

This is the case-note request. The interceptor never handles the file itself. It checks the presigned URL and hands it to Skyflow Detect, which returns a link to a clean copy.

Recent findings suggest that figure 4: Shield the document. The interceptor checks the presigned URL against the allowlist and size limit, Skyflow Detect fetches and de-identifies the file, and the agent receives a link to the clean copy.

Here is the case note as stored in Amazon S3, beside the copy the agent receives:.

Figure 5: The case note as stored (left) and the de-identified copy the agent receives (right).

A token like [NAME_AJbrIud] is a vault token, which an authorized user can reverse through Skyflow. A token like [NAME_1] is a one-way counter that nothing can reverse.

Recent findings suggest that the following video indicates Shield the document end to end. The agent asks for the dispute case note and receives a link to a de-identified copy instead of the original.

According to recent reports, video 1: Shield the document in action. Without Skyflow, the agent reads the original case note. With Skyflow on the gateway, it reads a de-identified copy.

The interceptor complements the controls AgentCore and Amazon Bedrock already provide:.

Industry observers note that the Skyflow interceptor is open source in the agentcore-skyflow repository on GitHub under the MIT license. Skyflow is available in AWS Marketplace. To add the interceptor to a gateway you already run:.

The repository also contains the complete reference deployment from this post, including the agent, the gateway, and its targets, which you can deploy with the AgentCore CLI, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

Skyflow offers several vault deployment models and Region choices to meet residency requirements. See Skyflow deployment models.

Recent findings suggest that agents are only as trustworthy as the data they move. With AgentCore Gateway and the Skyflow interceptor, you can enforce a privacy control at the one place every tool call passes through. It works in both directions, covers documents and text, and needs no change to agent code.

arXiv:2608.21274v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study an experiment with 8.5 million users on Netflix's recommender system to measure how improvements in recommendation technology affect the set of products that get consumed. Improvements increase total consumption and users' reliance on recommendations while diffusing recommendations and consumption away from the most popular titles ("superstars") toward a larger number of moderately popular titles ("middle-tail"), with minimal effects on the most niche titles ("long-tail"). Our results challenge the notion that recommender systems polarize consumption -- raising the consumption shares of the head and tail at the expense of the middle -- and suggest that the returns to investing in middle-tail products grow as algorithms improve and platforms scale.

KV-LTM: Persistent Per-Session KV Caches as Long-Term Memory for Personal Assistants

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (269 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.21998v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Personal assistants accumulate months of conversations, but today's long-term memory stacks put derivation or selection between a question and its evidence. In a system-level comparison on LongMemEval, two commercial assistants scored well below the same model reading the history offline [1], consistent with, but not isolating, content loss between write and read. We propose KV-LTM: a memory tier storing each session's raw text plus its KV cache under a fixed reader model, answering by restoring cached sessions and appending the question. KV-LTM is complementary to, not a replacement for, retrieval and indexing. Text is the memory of record; the cache is a recompute-free prefill accelerator, degrading gracefully to text. We specify the design: storage record, budget-derived retention, append-only read path, and bounded aggregation. We size it analytically: across pinned BF16 full-attention (GQA) and latent-cached MLA configurations, per-token state spans approximately 31K-328K bytes (the pinned KDA+MLA hybrid differs: approximately 8.1K bytes/token plus a fixed per-session recurrent term), giving approximately 0.34-3.6 TB per user-year at a declared 30K-token/day scenario, against approximately 49 MB of raw text; per-query cost is modelled as regime-conditional transfer, attention, decode, aggregation, and compute. We define an evaluation protocol needing no persistent-cache implementation for logical QA evaluation: per-session prefill emulates valid cache reuse under the same model/input-state contract and ideal arithmetic, with named arms, controlled baselines, and a preregistered reader-model gate; a separate minimal real-cache replay tests numerical equivalence and measures the cost axis, with outcomes not assumed. KV-LTM trades storage for avoided re-prefill compute and write-time fidelity, within a declared retention budget.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:.

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Industry observers note that results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where fresh models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:.

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:.

Industry observers note that of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:.

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:.

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

#4033. Keep inference running through regional capacity shortfalls with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2129 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Keep inference running through regional capacity shortfalls with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2129 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Serving a model from more than one AWS Region is a well-established pattern for highly available inference: when one Region runs short of GPU capacity, requests move to another.
  • Today, we’re introducing cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI.
  • Industry observers note that in this post, we explain how cross-Region inference routing decides where each request runs, walk through an example with one model in two Regions, and cover monitoring, limits, and what you pay.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Serving a model from more than one AWS Region is a well-established pattern for highly available inference: when one Region runs short of GPU capacity, requests move to another. The pattern is simple to describe and hard to operate. Until now, if you served models on Amazon SageMaker AI managed endpoints, cross-Region routing was a piece you still had to build yourself.

Today, we’re introducing cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI. It uses a latest resource, the inference router, that gives your application one invocation path across the endpoints and inference components you already run, in one or more AWS Regions and AWS accounts. You register the destinations that serve a model, and your application invokes the router instead of a specific endpoint. The router keeps requests in its own Region while the local destination is healthy, shifts new requests to another registered destination when it isn’t, and returns traffic gradually after recovery.

Industry observers note that in this post, we explain how cross-Region inference routing decides where each request runs, walk through an example with one model in two Regions, and cover monitoring, limits, and what you pay. For a cross-account deployment that serves several models, see How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI.

Sources indicate that A SageMaker AI endpoint runs in one AWS Region and one account. When autoscaling can’t add instances of the type your endpoint needs, requests throttle and time out, even when the same model has spare capacity in another Region. To use that capacity, your application must detect a struggling endpoint and switch Regions, decide which errors are safe to retry without running the model twice, move traffic back after recovery without flapping, and manage access to endpoints in other accounts. That code sits on the critical path of every request, and every team serving models across Regions maintains its own version of it.

Cross-Region inference routing is based on a few core ideas:.

A few terms describe the pieces:.

The Region you create the router in is its local Region. To prefer a different Region, create a router there. The router doesn’t create capacity, scale your endpoints, deploy models, or copy model artifacts and container images. Each destination must already be running in its Region.

Figure 1: Each request goes to a healthy destination, with the router preferring destinations in its own Region.

The router considers only destinations that are registered on the routing target and that it’s authorized to invoke. Among those, it prefers destinations in its own Region, and when more than one local destination is healthy, it spreads requests across them evenly. Requests leave the Region only when local destinations can’t serve reliably. To detect that, SageMaker AI calculates a health score for each destination from its recent requests, measured in the destination’s own Region. Server errors (5xx), throttles, and timeouts lower the score. Errors from the SageMaker AI platform (for example, failed health check) lower it the most. Errors caused by the request itself, such as invalid input, don’t lower it, because the same request would fail in any Region. Model latency isn’t an input, so an endpoint that keeps returning successful responses keeps its traffic. Signals such as failed instance launches or an endpoint running fewer instances than its autoscaling target make the router react faster, but only after the destination starts failing requests.

The router evaluates each destination’s health and publishes it to Amazon CloudWatch as one of three states. A healthy destination serves normally. An overloaded destination still serves, and the router moves part of its traffic away. A degraded destination is failing or can’t serve, so the router moves most of its traffic away and keeps a small share to detect recovery.

Figure 2: How each destination health state changes the traffic the router sends to it.

In a recent development, sageMaker AI manages failover thresholds and timing, so you don’t need to tune any thresholds. If health information for remote destinations goes stale, the router keeps traffic in its own Region, so a gap in monitoring never moves traffic on its own.

Sources indicate that the more requests fail, the more traffic moves, so a destination need not fail outright first. Traffic starts to move within about a minute of sustained errors, or longer for a destination with little traffic. Traffic that leaves the local Region is spread across the healthy remote destinations in proportion to their health. You can’t set weights or a fallback order. After recovery, traffic returns over several minutes, more slowly than it left. Requests in progress aren’t interrupted.

When a destination fails a real-time request without running the model, the router retries that request once on a different destination. This covers, for example, a throttle, a 503 error, a model that isn’t ready, a rejection by a cross-Region traffic cap, or access denied by the destination. The router never retries timeouts, 500 errors, or model errors.

For asynchronous requests, the router tries each eligible destination once, local destinations first, until one accepts the request.

Figure 3: The router retries a real-time request once on another destination, and only when the model didn’t run.

Figure 4 reveals where requests were served in one of our tests with a test model.

Figure 4: Where requests were served as the local endpoint was overloaded, a destination in another account lost and regained access, and the local endpoint recovered.

The following use cases show common ways to use cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI.

According to recent reports, when a destination belongs to a different account than the router, both accounts must allow each request. On the endpoint side, the owner attaches a resource-based policy that allows the router account to invoke the endpoint, and the sagemaker:SourceInferenceRouterArn condition key limits that access to one named router. The following policy allows only my-router in account 444455556666 to invoke the endpoint. Its second statement has no router condition and lets the router account read the endpoint’s status. Without that statement, the destination highlights its status as unknown.

Industry observers note that in the router account, callers need sagemaker:InvokeInferenceRouter (or sagemaker:InvokeInferenceRouterAsync) on the router and sagemaker:InvokeEndpoint (or sagemaker:InvokeEndpointAsync) on every destination, because the router invokes each destination on the caller’s behalf. A router never gives a caller access to an endpoint they couldn’t call directly. For DescribeInferenceRouter to report each destination’s status, callers also need sagemaker:DescribeEndpoint on endpoints and sagemaker:DescribeInferenceComponent on inference components. Applications in other accounts call the router by assuming a role in the router account. For a walkthrough, see How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI and User Guide on cross-account destinations.

Figure 5: Controls the endpoint owner keeps: an endpoint policy that allows one named router, and an optional cross-Region traffic cap.

Industry observers note that when the router moves requests away from a Region that’s short on capacity, those requests land on endpoints that already serve their own Region’s callers. By default, a receiving endpoint accepts any amount of cross-Region traffic, so a surge of overflow can push it into throttling. With a cross-Region traffic cap, the endpoint owner decides how much of the endpoint’s capacity other Regions might use.

According to recent reports, you set the cap in CreateEndpointConfig with CrossRegionTrafficConfig, which takes two required values. MaxInvocationsPerSecondPerInstance is the number of invocations per second that one instance can take, which you measure with a load test of your model, instance type, and typical payload. MaxCrossRegionPercentPerEndpoint is the share of that capacity that other Regions might use. SageMaker AI multiplies the per-instance rate by the instances in service and applies the percentage, so the cap follows autoscaling. For example, with 50 invocations per second per instance, a 20 percent cap, and 4 instances in service, the endpoint accepts up to 40 requests per second from other Regions. When autoscaling adds 2 instances, the cap rises to 60 requests per second.

Only requests from other Regions count against the cap. Requests from the endpoint’s own Region, including direct InvokeEndpoint calls and calls from a router in the same Region, are never throttled by it. When cross-Region requests exceed the cap, the endpoint rejects the extra requests before your model runs, and the router retries each one once on a different destination. If no other destination can take the request, your application gets a throttling error.

The cap applies to real-time endpoints, and all inference components on an endpoint share it. For an endpoint that hosts inference components, load test one instance with its usual mix of inference components and payloads to measure MaxInvocationsPerSecondPerInstance, and run the test again when that mix or your payloads change. If you leave out CrossRegionTrafficConfig, the endpoint accepts any amount of cross-Region traffic.

Recent findings suggest that in this example, we deploy Qwen3-4B with the vLLM container as an inference component in US East (Ohio) and US West (Oregon), in one account. Because the inference router doesn’t support response streaming, the application sends non-streaming requests, and each request must complete within about a minute, the same limit as InvokeEndpoint. We then create a router in US East (Ohio) with one routing target that lists both:.

Run DescribeInferenceRouter and confirm that each destination’s RoutingStatus is Routable before you send traffic.

The application invokes the router with the routing target name and the same payload it would send to InvokeEndpoint, and reads the serving destination and routing reason from the response:.

Traffic stayed in US East (Ohio) while its inference component ran, moved to US West (Oregon) with no change to the application when we removed it, and came back after we restored it.

The complete notebook for this example is available on GitHub.

According to recent reports, tip: Use instance pools and cross-Region inference routing together. With a capacity-aware instance pool, SageMaker AI can use another instance type in the same Region at creation and during scale-out. The router moves fresh requests to another Region when the local endpoint as a whole can’t serve. For details, see Capacity-aware inference: Automatic instance fallback for SageMaker AI endpoints.

The inference router gives you two views of routing: a record on every real-time response and metrics in CloudWatch.

Every real-time response includes the ARN of the destination that served the request in InvokedRoutedResourceArn, and the routing reason in RoutingReason. The routing reason is one of the following:.

We recommend logging both values with your application’s own request logs.

It has been revealed that asynchronous responses don’t include the serving destination. Router metrics in CloudWatch show where asynchronous requests were placed.

The router publishes OpenTelemetry metrics to CloudWatch in its own account and Region, labeled with the router, routing target, and destination:.

Sources indicate that alarm on destinations that aren’t healthy and on the error rate across all error types. See Monitor an inference routers with Amazon CloudWatch and AWS CloudTrail.

Figure 6: Requests per destination from the router’s CloudWatch invocations metric during the test shown in Figure 4.

Industry observers note that each destination endpoint keeps publishing its existing SageMaker AI metrics in its own account and Region. To view them in one place, use CloudWatch cross-account observability and cross-account cross-Region dashboards.

It has been revealed that AWS CloudTrail records the router’s API calls (create, revision, delete, describe, and list) as management events and router invocations as data events. You enable data events on your trail as you do for other SageMaker AI data events.

Keep the following in mind when you design with the inference router:.

Also note the following limitations:.

Industry observers note that cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI gives your application one invocation path across the endpoints and inference components you already run, in multiple AWS Regions and AWS accounts. The router prefers its own Region, shifts new requests when a destination can’t serve reliably, returns traffic gradually after recovery, and indicates you where each request ran and why. Your endpoints, models, containers, and autoscaling policies don’t change.

Cross-Region inference routing is generally available starting today in most commercial AWS Regions (except me-south-1 and me-central-1), for real-time and asynchronous inference.

In a recent development, there is no additional charge for cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI. You pay for the SageMaker AI endpoints and inference components that serve your requests at standard SageMaker AI pricing, whether a request reaches them directly or through an inference router. The inference router publishes metrics to Amazon CloudWatch in the router’s account, and you pay standard CloudWatch rates for those metrics and any queries you run on them. For details, see Amazon SageMaker AI pricing.

To get started, see the Amazon SageMaker AI documentation on cross-Region inference routing and explore the sample notebook on GitHub.

arXiv:2611.21978v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Large language models are moving from isolated assistants toward autonomous agents that can initiative, use tools, and coordinate with others, motivating an emerging Agentic Web of independently developed agents and services. Realizing this vision requires agent behavior to move across creators, hosts, and runtimes without coupling publication to a particular execution environment or transferring authority over user resources. We introduce WebAgents, which unbundles these roles through a signed agent.pkg that carries portable workflows, skills, schemas, and resource requirements. An OpenClaw-based agent-native browser/runtime verifies the package, obtains authorization, and binds it at run time to user-controlled models, tools, permissions, and budgets, while hosts distribute the public program and may retain private services server-side. We demonstrate this contract with three unrelated workflows executed unchanged under local and API-backed models, including literature review with live services and a website-published travel agent using semantic tools and user-selected personal resources. In a controlled suite, WebAgents explicitly blocks all 716 injected contract violations while accepting all 295 matched benign controls, with median automated pre-execution processing below 0.5 s for all three packages. We conclude by outlining a path toward NANDA-based discovery and interoperable package ecosystems while retaining execution authority in the user's runtime.

#4029. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1744 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1744 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one.
  • Recent findings suggest that both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language.
  • Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Recent findings suggest that both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer looks the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

Industry observers note that it lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Sources indicate that nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:.

According to recent reports, each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

Sources indicate that there's no public corpus of looks, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Sources indicate that every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:.

Industry observers note that "Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance.".

The coder reasons about geometry:.

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart.".

Industry observers note that the teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

Recent findings suggest that the hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

In a recent development, what fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the initiative and wrapped in [[ ]]:.

It has been revealed that the designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

It has been revealed that the model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Recent findings suggest that figure 1. An illustration of the same proposal without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

In a recent development, even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

In a recent development, the key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Recent findings suggest that figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

Recent findings suggest that to measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Recent findings suggest that palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

It has been revealed that presentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

It has been revealed that the harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2607.04753v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Narratives often combine diagnostic evidence with truthful but nondiagnostic details. In a two-state experiment with known signal likelihoods, we test whether such details distort belief updating. Although Bayes' rule prescribes no revision, nondiagnostic signals induce revisions consistent with considering both states equally likely. Such revisions are most frequent when nondiagnostic signals appear as clues in a story, less frequent in an abstract urn problem, and virtually absent when the same story replaces these clues with explicit no-information messages. Simulations show that these revisions reduce belief accuracy and delay decisions, an effect communicators could exploit without lying.

Mr. Stephen Quinn joined the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in 2004 and serves as a senior computer scientist in the Information Technology Laboratory (ITL). Mr. Quinn is the lead author for Integrating NIST risk management project work within the paradigm of Enterprise Risk Management (ERM). He is also program manager for the National Checklist Program and the National Online Informative Reference (OLIR) programs at NIST. He is a co-originator of the NIST Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP).

In a recent development, stephen was named to the “Federal 100” by the trade publication Federal Computer Week (FCW) and received the Department of Commence Gold Medal Award for his work in automating security protocols for applications. He also received the Federal CIO Council Leadership award for related work.

Prior to joining NIST, Steve worked in the private sector as a consultant to the Department of Defense and large commercial outsourcings with Wall Street banking firms and insurance companies. Specifically, he comes from an operational background, having owned two companies that provided service offering for vulnerability assessments, designing security architectures, code development, risk management, certifications and accreditations, and ST&Es. His research experience and practitioner experience includes managing and remediating risks specific to computer viruses/malware, intrusion detection systems (IDSs), vulnerability/misconfiguration identification, categorization, and remediation.

arXiv:2611.21950v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: AI agents can assist scientific research, but balancing autonomous investigation with scientists' ability to inspect and redirect ongoing work remains a central design challenge. We present DiscoveryAgent, a domain-agnostic, scientist-centric system that combines autonomous investigation with scientist-directed hypothesis steering. Scientists select, refine, or replace hypotheses between research rounds, while audit agents interrogate checkpointed records to trace claims, reproduce analyses, and inform subsequent decisions. Across two predictive modeling tasks, DiscoveryAgent produced the best variable-star classifier among evaluated baselines and, with scientist steering, a protein variant-effect predictor surpassed by only one of 106 ProteinGym baselines. We develop a rigorous checkpointing system that enables highly capable audit agents, a scalable form of oversight for agentic research. Audit agents autonomously identify errors at higher rates than previous AI scientist agents, and scientists collaborating with audit agents identify 14x more valid errors versus scientists performing manual review. In three case studies led by domain experts across physical science, social science, and life science, we developed a multimodal photometric-redshift estimator that resolves complementary failures of images and photometry, achieving 0.971 AUROC for low-redshift classification; documented an 83% rise in Florida homeowners-insurance premiums from 2013 to 2023, with a growing, regressive burden; and identified CD4+ T-cell relay genes, which both receive and exert broad transcriptional regulation, enriched for autoimmune disease associations. Together, these results show how autonomous research can expand scientists' empirical reach while centering their authority over research direction and their ability to understand and challenge the evidence.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that cisco, like many large engineering organizations, is adopting generative and agentic AI to change how its engineers build software. The hard part is no longer access to the technology. It’s helping thousands of engineers move from watching a demo to confidently building with it. Recorded sessions and slide decks rarely close that gap. Engineers learn fastest when they build something real, see it fail, fix it, and try again.

In a recent development, AWS designed AWS AI League for exactly that. It turns hands-on AI learning into a gamified competition, where participants customize models and build agents on AWS, get instant feedback on a live leaderboard, and compete in a game-show-style finale.

Sources indicate that cisco is one of the clearest examples of what this looks like at scale. In 2025, Hemanth V, a Cisco software engineer, went from an internal Cisco event to being crowned the first AWS AI League Champion at AWS re:Invent 2025. In 2026, 1,200 Cisco engineers competed in an AWS AI League tournament at Cisco Transformation Fest 4.0. The winner, Nishanth Aluhonnu, earned a full event pass to AWS re:Invent 2026 in Las Vegas.

Industry observers note that in this post, we share how Cisco and AWS used Cisco Transformation Fest and AWS AI League to build a lasting culture of learning by doing. We previously covered this program in From theory to delivery: How Atos upskilled 400 engineers in agentic AI, and here we look at Cisco’s experience. We walk through Cisco’s journey, share technical lessons from the 2026 winning agent, and explain how your organization can host its own AWS AI League.

Industry observers note that AWS AI League helps organizations build advanced AI skills through competition. Each league follows three steps:.

Although AWS AI League offers multiple use cases, at Cisco it offered the following two challenges:.

Finalists are scored on time efficiency, accuracy, agent planning, and token consumption efficiency.

Figure 1: AWS AI League champion at AWS re:Invent 2025.

Figure 2: 2026 AWS AI League winner at Cisco campus.

Industry observers note that the AWS AI League story at Cisco grows out of a deep engineering partnership. Cisco and AWS bring together networking, cloud, security, and observability for shared customers including:.

The two companies have also published joint deployment guides and Cisco Validated Designs across networking and AWS. A recent example of co-innovation is SD-WAN fabric on demand across the AWS backbone, built to deliver the resilience and uptime customers expect.

According to recent reports, “When you see that many business units independently choosing to build their next-generation platforms natively on AWS, that’s not a vendor relationship anymore. It’s a true engineering partnership.”.

— Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco.

Cisco’s VP of Engineering Kumaril Kapoor and AWS Industries India leader Chandra Balani sit down to discuss the AWS and Cisco partnership story, from co-innovation across networking, cloud, and AI to enabling thousands of engineers through the annual Cisco AWS Transformation Fest.

Recent findings suggest that as the partnership grew, it extended beyond technology to people. Working closely with Cisco teams in India, AWS saw a strong appetite for learning and experimenting among Cisco engineers across many business units. The question was how to scale that impact beyond the day-to-day touchpoints of the partnership.

Industry observers note that the answer was Cisco Transformation Fest, first held in 2022. The program is built on five tenets the team summarized as SCALE:.

Figure 3: 2026 Cisco AWS Transformation Fest 4.0 AWS AI League finalists.

Transformation Fest brings together several formats: AWS GameDays, AWS AI League, sessions where Cisco leaders share best practices and success stories with peers, and sessions on Amazon and AWS culture. What began as a single event is now an annual, three-day program that has completed its fourth edition and reached around 2,000 engineers. AWS continues to engage Cisco teams with hands-on workshops and experience-based accelerations.

Sources indicate that “It has been genuinely valuable for us, and it’s really a journey, but I appreciate most is the intent behind it. It’s built around our people. It gives our engineers the time, the space, and the hands-on support to grow real skills on AWS. For us, it has turned into a lasting culture of learning by doing. It’s not a one-off event.”.

— Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco.

It has been revealed that of all the Transformation Fest formats, AWS AI League has had the most visible impact. Its gamified, hands-on structure puts engineers to work with Amazon SageMaker on fine-tuning, model customization and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for agent building, against a clock and in front of their peers. Participants leave with practical experience and genuine confidence in their AI skills.

“This is where enablement actually turns into real execution.”.

— Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco.

Hemanth V, a software engineer in Cisco’s switching core platform team, had an inspiring journey that set the benchmark for Cisco.

Hemanth finished ahead of Ross Williams from Aqfer (second place) and Deepesh Khanna from Capital One (third place).

It has been revealed that “You don’t need to know everything beforehand. You will learn a lot of things on the way. The only thing that matters is your curiosity and willingness to learn.”.

— Hemanth V, Software Engineer, Cisco, and 2025 AWS AI League Champion.

In 2026, Cisco Transformation Fest 4.0 hosted a full AWS AI League agentic AI tournament. The AWS account team ran pre-event training so that engineers with no prior agentic AI experience could compete from day one. The format was designed to narrow a large field down to a single winner:.

Nishanth Aluhonnu, a software engineer at Cisco, finished first at every stage and earned a full conference pass to AWS re:Invent 2026.

The finale itself highlighted why the format works. Participants could not change code, tools, or prompts during the finale, only a short steering instruction before each round. Success depended on how well each agent made decisions on maps it had never seen before. Nishanth lost the first round, then won the second by a wide margin by ignoring a board full of low-value coins in favor of a single high-value challenge.

Figure 4: Cisco AWS Transformation Fest 4.0 AWS AI League finalists on stage.

Recent findings suggest that the 2026 winning agent offers lessons that go well beyond the game. Each design choice maps to a decision teams face when they run agents in production.

The agentic AI challenge scores agents on challenge points, a treasure bonus, remaining lives, and a token bonus, computed as tokenBonus = 1000 - (totalOutputTokens / challengesVisited).

In the qualifier, the top four agents all solved the map. The first-place agent emitted 1,220 output tokens and the second-place agent emitted 1,430, and the final margin was only 16 points out of nearly 16,000. After every agent can solve the problem, efficiency decides the winner.

To understand which tokens mattered, Nishanth built nine variants of the same agent, changing one thing at a time. The result was clear: tool results and the system prompt didn’t count against the score, but everything the agent wrote, including tool call arguments, did. Each tool call carried roughly 52 tokens of fixed overhead on top of its arguments.

Sources indicate that this mirrors real-world cost. Generating output is sequential and is typically priced several times higher than input, and in an agent loop that cost compounds across every step. A long, well-structured system prompt (which you can also cache) is cheap. A chatty agent isn’t.

A common architecture for this challenge is a supervisor agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that delegates to specialist sub-agents for navigation, computation, and web retrieval. It’s a sound pattern for many production systems. The winning design used a single agent with no sub-agents. Instead, the prompt began with a short dispatch table that matched each challenge type to the right approach in a single turn.

Recent findings suggest that the reasoning was simple: every handoff between agents is a message the model has to write, and in this challenge every written token is scored. The lesson isn’t that sub-agents are bad. It’s to choose your architecture based on what coordination costs you. When coordination is expensive, a flatter design can win.

In a recent development, the following diagram indicates the AWS reference architecture for the agentic AI challenge: a supervisor agent with specialist sub-agents. The winning design deliberately didn’t use this multi-agent pattern.

Figure 5: AWS AI League reference architecture.

In this reference architecture, a supervisor agent runs in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and coordinates three sub-agents, with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and AgentCore memory connected to the runtime. The supervisor and sub-agents route through the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to four tools: a navigation tool, browser tool, code execution tool, and custom tools using AWS Lambda functions.

Route planning was not left to the model. It ran in an AWS Lambda function that treated the board as an optimization problem. Each tile carried an expected value: the points it paid, minus the lives it could cost, minus the tokens the agent would spend to solve it. The planner respected constraints, such as collecting a key before its door, and refined the route within a time budget.

This is a useful pattern for most agents: let the model handle language and judgment, and move search, math, and rules into tools where they are faster, cheaper, and repeatable.

The second finale round was designed as a trap. A seven-by-seven board was almost entirely covered in coins worth 25 points each, while a single scheduling challenge tile was worth 1,500 points. Habit mentioned to collect the coins. The planner’s value table said the coins were noise. The agent went for the high-value challenge and scored 7,537 points in that round, compared with 5,953 for the next finalist. That round built the lead that carried the agent to the overall win.

Across two years of AWS AI League at Cisco, the impact indicates up in skills, culture, and recognition:.

For Hemanth, the biggest takeaway was confidence. You do not need to master everything before you start. You learn by getting hands-on.

It has been revealed that “Technology alone isn’t enough. You need people who are empowered to experiment with it. Transformation Fest created that enablement environment, and AWS AI League created the opportunity for execution.”.

— Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco.

Recent findings suggest that in this post, we demonstrated how Cisco and AWS turned enablement into execution. Cisco Transformation Fest created a space for engineers to learn by doing, and AWS AI League gave them a real challenge, a scoreboard, and a stage. The result is a culture of hands-on AI building that reaches thousands of engineers.

We look forward to seeing what your teams build.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2509.03964v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In traditional finance, liquid markets for bonds, interest rate swaps, and other interest rate derivatives provide a basis for constructing yield curves. In the cryptocurrency ecosystem, lending and staking yields are predominantly variable and adjust over short timescales, whereas fixed-rate instruments remain scarce and, as of early 2026, widely accepted benchmark yield curves were still lacking. We jointly infer USD and cryptocurrency discount factors from inverse options and futures by combining put-call parity with the futures basis in a closed-form estimator. We introduce a novel RANSAC-based quote filter tailored to cryptocurrency market microstructure. We apply the method to hourly BTC and ETH derivatives data from Deribit between February~2023 and February~2026. The two underlying assets imply broadly similar USD term structures, with rates averaging approximately 8\% per year and rising during the 2024 cryptocurrency rallies. Implied BTC and ETH rates are typically close to zero across the maturities considered, despite positive Aave lending yields and ETH staking yields. Implied USD rates co-move with Aave USDC rates but exhibit persistent differences. These findings suggest limited integration between derivatives markets and decentralized lending and staking.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

According to recent reports, in April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

In a recent development, OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

Recent findings suggest that however, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Recent findings suggest that run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that promptly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

According to recent reports, say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:.

Recent findings suggest that the choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a fresh 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:.

It has been revealed that all three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

According to recent reports, the full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

Sources indicate that this is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

It has been revealed that this isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

It has been revealed that parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

Explore Dharma AI on Hugging Face to try our interactive demos, download our open-source models, and discover how specialized AI systems outperform general-purpose models in real enterprise applications.
